newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Wage arrears at Moscow nuclear centre raise fears.
newsitem.headline: Wage arrears at Moscow nuclear centre raise fears.

text.p: Physicists at Russia's top nuclear institute, which runs eight research reactors just 10 km (six miles) from the Kremlin, have not been paid in four months, raising fears about safety in Moscow, officials said on Tuesday.

"Of course, if we do not get wages for a long time, we cannot be sure that our people will work well and carefully," said Andrei Gagarinsky, head of the Kurchatov Institute's foreign relations department. "It's one serious problem."

Russia's State Duma lower house of parliament -- which has a radiation counter near the entrance -- last week adopted a resolution expressing serious concern about the risk of radiation from the institute because of underfunding.

During a tour of the Kurchatov Institute on Tuesday, physicists and support staff complained about their wage arrears but all refused to predict imminent ecological disaster, theft of nuclear fuel or an exodus of experts for rogue countries.
"It's very hard for us," said Vladimir Ushkov, head of the laboratory for accelerator physics.
"But I don't think professionals who worked here their whole lives would allow a fall in standards or theft."
Founded in 1943 in what was then a forest well outside Moscow, the institute long attracted Russia's leading minds. It now sits in a northern suburb surrounded by apartment blocks.

Even after the fall of communism the staff got regular pay while other enterprises faltered. But late last year the institute fell behind on its payments and arrears on average monthly wages of under $100 date have built up since October.

Little cash means that reactors are fired up about twice a month to conduct experiments, Gagarinsky said. The oldest model dates back half a century and in its single-storey, faded pink brick facade resembles a storage shed in sore need of repair.

At the accelerator physics lab, 50 people work where 200 once did research, officials said. "We live in such an era. What are we going to do, hang ourselves?" asked Lev Yudin, head of one team, who gives physics lessons to boost his income.
About 3,000 of the Kurchatov Institute's workers have left since 1990, leaving 7,000 behind, Gagarinsky said. Only a few have permanently gone abroad, with one to South Africa, he said.
"I don't want to work in North Korea, Iraq or Libya. I want to work at home," Ushkov said, referring to countries that western experts fear are trying to develop nuclear weapons.
But the institute itself will collaborate with any country, and earns about $2.5 million annually on top of its $12 million government budget from outside contracts, Gagarinsky said.

"We are ready to help any country without exception," he said. But only, he added, in compliance with the nuclear arms Non-Proliferation Treaty. "If we do not help them, somebody else will help them, and of course they can do it themselves."

In recent years Libya has expressed an interest in re-establishing its Soviet-built nuclear research centre, and Syria has made inquiries, but no deals were concluded, Gagarinsky said. Iran recently sent experts for training as part of a deal to build a nuclear power plant in Bushehr, he added.
On the long term, however, some experts say the Kurchatov nuclear reactors should be closed to assure Moscow's safety.
"It's not right to have them so close to the Kremlin. Russia is a big country and there's a lot of other places for reactors," Ushkov said.
But it would take years to dismantle the facilities even if Russia could afford to do so immediately, physicists say.
"It's a question of what's cheaper: to close down the reactor and move them somewhere else, or keep them working today," said Yudin.
